kana.note: A long i is written by simply repeating the kana: おおきい, ちいさい.

う also writes vowel length: added after an o-column kana it makes a long o (とうきょう = Tokyo), and after a u-column kana a long u (ゆうめい). Modified Hepburn writes these as o and u with a macron, not as "ou".

A long o is normally written おう (とうきょう), but a short list of words writes it おお instead: おおきい (big), おおい (many), とおい (far), おおさか (Osaka). There is no rule to derive this from — the おお words are learned as a list.

kana.printVsHandwritten: Many printed faces join the last two strokes of き into one sweep. The handwritten form keeps the final stroke separate — four strokes, not three.
Printed さ often joins the second and third strokes into one curve. Handwritten さ keeps the bottom curve detached from the vertical.

kana.note: Romanised shi, never "si" — the consonant is not the same sound as in さ. An IME accepts either spelling.

kana.printVsHandwritten: Two accepted shapes. Most printed faces draw そ as one continuous stroke; handwriting is often taught with the top horizontal written separately (two strokes). Both are correct — KanjiVG documents the one-stroke form, which is what the app animates.

kana.note: Romanised chi. An IME produces it from either chi or ti.
Romanised tsu — one consonant sound, not "t + s". An IME produces it from tsu or tu.
Written は and read "ha" as a character — but when it marks the topic of a sentence it is pronounced "wa": わたしは がくせいです (watashi wa gakusei desu). The spelling never changes; only the sound does.

kana.printVsHandwritten: Printed ふ looks like one flowing shape. It is written as four separate strokes: the top tick, the left curve, then the two short strokes on the right.
kana.note: The h-row consonant becomes an f-like sound before u, so ふ is romanised fu. An IME accepts fu or hu.
Written へ and read "he" as a character — but as the particle marking a direction or destination it is pronounced "e": とうきょうへ いきます (Tokyo e ikimasu).
The r-row consonant is a single tap of the tongue — between an English r and l, and closer to a light d than to either.

kana.printVsHandwritten: Some printed faces join the two strokes of り into one shape. Handwritten り is two separate strokes.

kana.note: Spelled wo, pronounced "o". In modern Japanese を is used almost only as the object particle: ほんを よむ (hon o yomu). A word that starts with the "o" sound is written お, never を.

The only kana that is a consonant on its own, and it takes a full beat. Its sound follows what comes next: before b, p and m it is pronounced [m] — しんぶん (newspaper) sounds like "shimbun", えんぴつ like "empitsu". Typing it usually needs a doubled n: "kani" gives かに, "kanni" gives かんい. Hepburn writes n’ before a vowel to keep しんあい (shin’ai) distinct from しない.
ウ does double duty in loanwords: with a small vowel it writes the missing w-sounds (ウィ, ウェ, ウォ), and with dakuten it becomes ヴ for a foreign v.

kana.printVsHandwritten: Print does not show stroke direction, and シ is told apart from ツ by exactly that. シ: two short ticks stacked down the LEFT side, then a long stroke sweeping from lower left up to the right. ツ: two ticks along the TOP, then a long stroke sweeping down to the left.

Print does not show stroke direction. ソ and ン have the same short opening tick; they differ in the long second stroke. ソ: it starts top right and sweeps DOWN-LEFT, like ノ. ン: it starts at the left and sweeps DOWN-RIGHT, flicking up at the end, like the last stroke of シ.

Print does not show stroke direction, and ツ is told apart from シ by exactly that. ツ: two short ticks along the TOP, then a long stroke sweeping down to the LEFT. シ: ticks stacked down the left, final stroke sweeping up to the right.
kana.note: In loanwords ツ often stands in for a foreign tu (ツアー, tour); the dedicated トゥ spelling is newer and less common. The small ッ is the same shape at half size and doubles the next consonant instead.
テ plus a small ィ writes the ti sound Japanese has no kana for: パーティー, ティッシュ.
ト plus a small ゥ writes tu: タトゥー.
フ is the base of every foreign f sound: フ + a small vowel gives ファ, フィ, フェ, フォ.
Katakana ヘ and hiragana へ are nearly identical shapes; only context tells you which script you are reading.
Katakana ヲ is effectively obsolete: modern loanwords use ウォ for the wo sound. You will meet ヲ in pre-war documents and in stylised titles, not in everyday text.
The same syllabic n as hiragana ん, with the same [m] colouring before b, p and m: アンパン, テンプラ. Its shape is the classic katakana trap — see ソ for how the long stroke tells them apart.

The small っ writes consonant LENGTH, not a "tsu" sound. It holds the next consonant for one extra beat: きって (kitte, a stamp) against きて (kite, come); and いっぱい needs it where いぱい would be a different word shape. Romanised by doubling the following consonant. On an IME you get it by typing that doubled consonant (kitte), or directly with xtu / ltu.
Small ゃ. It is not written on its own in ordinary Japanese: it exists to build the contracted きゃ / しゅ / ちょ syllables, where it merges with the kana before it into one beat. Typed xya.
Small ゅ. It is not written on its own in ordinary Japanese: it exists to build the contracted きゃ / しゅ / ちょ syllables, where it merges with the kana before it into one beat. Typed xyu.
Small ょ. It is not written on its own in ordinary Japanese: it exists to build the contracted きゃ / しゅ / ちょ syllables, where it merges with the kana before it into one beat. Typed xyo.
Small ぁ. Hiragana almost never uses it: you meet it in written-out speech (あぁ) and in transcriptions. The katakana ァ is the one that matters, because it builds ファ, ティ, ウィ and friends. Typed xa.
Small ぃ. Hiragana almost never uses it: you meet it in written-out speech (あぁ) and in transcriptions. The katakana ィ is the one that matters, because it builds ファ, ティ, ウィ and friends. Typed xi.
Small ぅ. Hiragana almost never uses it: you meet it in written-out speech (あぁ) and in transcriptions. The katakana ゥ is the one that matters, because it builds ファ, ティ, ウィ and friends. Typed xu.
Small ぇ. Hiragana almost never uses it: you meet it in written-out speech (あぁ) and in transcriptions. The katakana ェ is the one that matters, because it builds ファ, ティ, ウィ and friends. Typed xe.
Small ぉ. Hiragana almost never uses it: you meet it in written-out speech (あぁ) and in transcriptions. The katakana ォ is the one that matters, because it builds ファ, ティ, ウィ and friends. Typed xo.

Same consonant-length mark as hiragana っ, and just as common in loanwords: サッカー (soccer), コップ (cup), チケット (ticket). Romanised by doubling the next consonant; typed as that doubled consonant, or as xtu / ltu.

The long-vowel mark. It lengthens the vowel of the kana before it: コーヒー (kōhī, coffee), ラーメン, ケーキ. It is a katakana convention — hiragana does not use it in ordinary writing, and lengthens a vowel instead by writing the vowel again (おおきい) or by adding う (とうきょう). Typed as the hyphen key. Written vertically it becomes a vertical line, not a rotated dash.
Small ャ. It is not written on its own in ordinary Japanese: it exists to build the contracted キャ / シュ / チョ syllables, where it merges with the kana before it into one beat. Typed xya.
Small ュ. It is not written on its own in ordinary Japanese: it exists to build the contracted キャ / シュ / チョ syllables, where it merges with the kana before it into one beat. Typed xyu.
Small ョ. It is not written on its own in ordinary Japanese: it exists to build the contracted キャ / シュ / チョ syllables, where it merges with the kana before it into one beat. Typed xyo.
Small ァ. Not a syllable on its own — it combines with the kana before it to write sounds Japanese has no kana for: フ + ァ in ファ / フィ / フェ / フォ, テ + ィ in ティ. Typed xa.
Small ィ. Not a syllable on its own — it combines with the kana before it to write sounds Japanese has no kana for: フ + ィ in ファ / フィ / フェ / フォ, テ + ィ in ティ. Typed xi.
Small ゥ. Not a syllable on its own — it combines with the kana before it to write sounds Japanese has no kana for: フ + ゥ in ファ / フィ / フェ / フォ, テ + ィ in ティ. Typed xu.
Small ェ. Not a syllable on its own — it combines with the kana before it to write sounds Japanese has no kana for: フ + ェ in ファ / フィ / フェ / フォ, テ + ィ in ティ. Typed xe.
Small ォ. Not a syllable on its own — it combines with the kana before it to write sounds Japanese has no kana for: フ + ォ in ファ / フィ / フェ / フォ, テ + ィ in ティ. Typed xo.
じ and ぢ are pronounced identically in modern standard Japanese. じ is the normal spelling and the one to use unless you know the word takes ぢ. Type ji or zi.
ず and づ are pronounced identically. ず is the normal spelling.

Sounds exactly like じ, and is romanised ji. It is written only where a ち has been voiced inside a word — by repetition, as in ちぢむ (to shrink), or by compounding, as in はなぢ (nosebleed, はな + ち). Everywhere else the correct spelling is じ. The IME key is di.

Sounds exactly like ず, and is romanised zu. It is written only where a つ has been voiced inside a word: つづく (to continue), つづける, みかづき (crescent moon, みか + つき). Everywhere else write ず. The IME key is du.
The h-row with a small circle instead of two dots. Two dots voice the consonant (ば), a circle makes it p (ぱ) — the two marks are easy to confuse at small sizes.
じ and ぢ are pronounced identically in modern standard Japanese. じ is the normal spelling and the one to use unless you know the word takes ぢ. Type ji or zi.
ず and づ are pronounced identically. ず is the normal spelling.

Sounds exactly like じ, and is romanised ji. It is written only where a ち has been voiced inside a word — by repetition, as in ちぢむ (to shrink), or by compounding, as in はなぢ (nosebleed, はな + ち). Everywhere else the correct spelling is じ. The IME key is di.

Sounds exactly like ず, and is romanised zu. It is written only where a つ has been voiced inside a word: つづく (to continue), つづける, みかづき (crescent moon, みか + つき). Everywhere else write ず. The IME key is du.
The h-row with a small circle instead of two dots. Two dots voice the consonant (ば), a circle makes it p (ぱ) — the two marks are easy to confuse at small sizes.
A full-size i-column kana plus a SMALL ゃ: one syllable, one beat. Compare きや (two beats) with きゃ (one).
Hepburn spells this sha, not "sya": the sound is the し consonant, not s + y. Both spellings work on an IME.
Hepburn spells this cha, not "tya". An IME accepts cha or tya.
Hepburn spells this ja. An IME accepts ja, jya or zya.
Pronounced exactly like じゃ. Almost never written: it survives in a few dialect and old-spelling forms, and inside compounds where a ちゃ is voiced. Use じゃ unless a dictionary shows otherwise.
Pronounced exactly like じゅ, and almost never written. Use じゅ.
Pronounced exactly like じょ, and almost never written. Use じょ.
A full-size i-column kana plus a SMALL ゃ: one syllable, one beat. Compare きや (two beats) with きゃ (one).
Hepburn spells this sha, not "sya": the sound is the し consonant, not s + y. Both spellings work on an IME.
Hepburn spells this cha, not "tya". An IME accepts cha or tya.
Hepburn spells this ja. An IME accepts ja, jya or zya.
Pronounced exactly like じゃ. Almost never written: it survives in a few dialect and old-spelling forms, and inside compounds where a ちゃ is voiced. Use じゃ unless a dictionary shows otherwise.
Pronounced exactly like じゅ, and almost never written. Use じゅ.
Pronounced exactly like じょ, and almost never written. Use じょ.
フ + small ァ for a foreign fa: ファイル (file), ファン (fan), ソファ (sofa).
フィルム (film), オフィス (office), フィンランド (Finland).
カフェ (cafe), フェリー (ferry), フェスティバル.
フォーク (fork), プラットフォーム, インフォメーション.
テ + small ィ for a foreign ti, which Japanese has no native syllable for: パーティー (party), チケット vs ティーシャツ, ティッシュ. Older borrowings used チ instead (チーム for "team"). The IME key is thi — plain ti gives ち.
ディスク (disc), ディズニー (Disney), メディア (media). The IME key is dhi — plain di gives ぢ.
ト + small ゥ for a foreign tu: タトゥー (tattoo), トゥモロー. Many words use ツ or ト instead. The IME key is twu — plain tu gives つ.
ヒンドゥー (Hindu), ドゥーワップ. Rarer than トゥ. The IME key is dwu.
ウ + small ィ for a foreign wi: ウィスキー (whisky), ウィンドウ (window), ウィキ. Some publishers still write ウイスキー with a full-size イ.
ウェブ (web), ウェイター, ハロウィン/ハロウェン. The historical kana for this sound was ヱ.
ウォーター (water), ストップウォッチ (stopwatch), ウォン (won). This, not ヲ, is how the wo sound is written in modern loanwords.

ウ with dakuten, used for a foreign v. Most loanwords now use the b-row instead (バイオリン rather than ヴァイオリン), and Japanese speakers usually pronounce ヴ as b anyway; the 1991 Cabinet notification on loanword spelling (外来語の表記) puts the b-row in its general table and ヴ in the table of accepted alternatives. You will still meet ヴ on its own in ラヴ (love), ライヴ (live) and イヴ (Eve).
ヴァイオリン (violin), ヴァージョン — both usually written バイオリン, バージョン today.
ヴィンテージ (vintage), ヴィクトリア (Victoria); commonly ビンテージ.
ヴェネツィア (Venice), ヴェルサイユ (Versailles); commonly ベネチア.
ヴォーカル (vocal), ヴォルガ (Volga); commonly ボーカル.
シェフ (chef), シェア (share), ミルクシェイク. The し consonant with an e vowel, which the gojuon table has no cell for.
ジェット (jet), ジェンダー, プロジェクト (project).
チェック (check), チェス (chess), チェロ (cello).
モーツァルト (Mozart), ピッツァ (pizza).
ライプツィヒ (Leipzig), ヴェネツィア (Venice). Chiefly in German and Italian names.
ツェッペリン (Zeppelin), コンツェルン (Konzern). Chiefly in German names and terms.
カンツォーネ (canzone), ピッツォ. Chiefly in Italian words.
ク + small ァ for a foreign kwa: クァルテット (quartet). Most such words are written with a plain カ or クア instead (カルテット, クアラルンプール), so this spelling is uncommon.
The same kwa sound written with a small ヮ instead of ァ. The older of the two spellings and now rare; you meet it in historical transcriptions and in Ryukyuan and dialect writing. Prefer クァ.
グァテマラ (Guatemala), グァム (Guam) — both also written グアテマラ, グアム with a full-size ア.
Marginal. Used in transcription of foreign names: キェルケゴール (Kierkegaard), also written キルケゴール. No everyday loanword uses it.
Marginal. It appears only in ad-hoc transcription of Slavic and Romance names; no established loanword uses it, and this inventory does not claim a standard example.
Marginal. Occasional in foreign-name transcription (most such names use ヒエ instead); no established loanword uses it.
Marginal. Occasional in Slavic name transcription; no established loanword uses it.
Marginal. Occasional in Slavic name transcription; no established loanword uses it.

Historical kana for wi. Its sound merged with い centuries ago, and the 1946 spelling reform removed it from ordinary use. You meet it in pre-war texts and in classical Japanese — never in modern spelling.
Historical kana for we. Its sound merged with え, and the 1946 reform removed it from ordinary use. Pre-war texts and classical Japanese only.
Historical katakana for wi, removed from ordinary use by the 1946 spelling reform. It survives in a few company and product names (the farm-machinery maker ヰセキ). Modern loanwords write this sound ウィ.
Historical katakana for we, removed from ordinary use by the 1946 reform. Best known from the beer brand ヱビス (Yebisu). Modern loanwords write this sound ウェ.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the five vowels
lessons.note: The five vowels. Every other kana is one of these with a consonant in front, so the five sounds a-i-u-e-o are the whole phonetic system in miniature. Japanese u is said with flat, unrounded lips.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the か row
Hiragana: the さ row
lessons.note: Watch the i-column: し is shi, not "si".

lessons.title: Hiragana: the た row
lessons.note: Two irregular cells here: ち is chi and つ is tsu, not "ti" and "tu".

lessons.title: Hiragana: the な row
Hiragana: the は row
lessons.note: ふ is fu, not "hu" — the consonant is lighter than an English f, made with the lips alone. は has a second life as the topic particle, where it is pronounced "wa".

lessons.title: Hiragana: the ま row
Hiragana: the や row
lessons.note: Only three cells: yi and ye do not exist in modern Japanese.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the ら row
lessons.note: One tapped consonant for the whole row, between an English r and l.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the わ row
lessons.note: A three-cell row, and the only one with leftovers: わ is a normal syllable, を survives only as the object particle (pronounced "o"), and ん is a consonant on its own.

lessons.title: Hiragana: small っ, ゃ, ゅ, ょ
lessons.note: Four half-size kana that change the beat rather than adding a sound: っ holds the next consonant, and ゃ/ゅ/ょ fuse with the kana before them. Size is the whole distinction — きや is two beats, きゃ is one.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the small vowels ぁぃぅぇぉ
lessons.note: Half-size vowels. Hiragana barely uses them; they are here so you recognise them, and because the katakana versions build every loanword sound Japanese lacks a kana for.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the が row
lessons.note: The か row with two dots. Voiced kana are never new shapes — learn the mark, not ten more characters.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the ざ row
lessons.note: じ is ji. ぢ in the だ row sounds the same but is almost never the right spelling.

lessons.title: Hiragana: the だ row
lessons.note: ぢ and づ sound exactly like じ and ず. They appear only where a ち or つ is voiced inside a word (ちぢむ, つづく).

lessons.title: Hiragana: the ば row
Hiragana: the ぱ row
lessons.note: The only row that uses the small circle (handakuten) instead of two dots.

lessons.title: Hiragana: きゃ きゅ きょ
Hiragana: しゃ しゅ しょ
Hiragana: ちゃ ちゅ ちょ
Hiragana: にゃ にゅ にょ
Hiragana: ひゃ ひゅ ひょ
Hiragana: みゃ みゅ みょ
Hiragana: りゃ りゅ りょ
Hiragana: ぎゃ ぎゅ ぎょ
Hiragana: じゃ じゅ じょ
Hiragana: びゃ びゅ びょ
Hiragana: ぴゃ ぴゅ ぴょ
Hiragana: ぢゃ ぢゅ ぢょ
lessons.note: Rare forms, included only so you can read them. They sound exactly like the じゃ set and are practically never the right spelling.

lessons.title: Katakana: the five vowels
lessons.note: The five vowels. Every other kana is one of these with a consonant in front, so the five sounds a-i-u-e-o are the whole phonetic system in miniature. Japanese u is said with flat, unrounded lips.

lessons.title: Katakana: the カ row
Katakana: the サ row
lessons.note: Watch the i-column: し is shi, not "si".

lessons.title: Katakana: the タ row
lessons.note: Two irregular cells here: ち is chi and つ is tsu, not "ti" and "tu".

lessons.title: Katakana: the ナ row
Katakana: the ハ row
lessons.note: ふ is fu, not "hu" — the consonant is lighter than an English f, made with the lips alone. は has a second life as the topic particle, where it is pronounced "wa".

lessons.title: Katakana: the マ row
Katakana: the ヤ row
lessons.note: Only three cells: yi and ye do not exist in modern Japanese.

lessons.title: Katakana: the ラ row
lessons.note: One tapped consonant for the whole row, between an English r and l.

lessons.title: Katakana: the ワ row
lessons.note: A three-cell row, and the only one with leftovers: わ is a normal syllable, を survives only as the object particle (pronounced "o"), and ん is a consonant on its own.

lessons.title: Katakana: ー, small ッ, ャ, ュ, ョ
lessons.note: The marks that make katakana work for loanwords: ー lengthens the vowel before it, ッ doubles the next consonant, and ャ/ュ/ョ fuse into one beat. コーヒー, サッカー, キャベツ.

lessons.title: Katakana: the small vowels ァィゥェォ
lessons.note: Half-size vowels. These are the building blocks of ファ, ティ, ウィ and ヴォ: a full-size kana keeps its consonant and borrows the small vowel.

lessons.title: Katakana: the ガ row
lessons.note: The か row with two dots. Voiced kana are never new shapes — learn the mark, not ten more characters.

lessons.title: Katakana: the ザ row
lessons.note: じ is ji. ぢ in the だ row sounds the same but is almost never the right spelling.

lessons.title: Katakana: the ダ row
lessons.note: ぢ and づ sound exactly like じ and ず. They appear only where a ち or つ is voiced inside a word (ちぢむ, つづく).

lessons.title: Katakana: the バ row
Katakana: the パ row
lessons.note: The only row that uses the small circle (handakuten) instead of two dots.

lessons.title: Katakana: キャ キュ キョ
Katakana: シャ シュ ショ
Katakana: チャ チュ チョ
Katakana: ニャ ニュ ニョ
Katakana: ヒャ ヒュ ヒョ
Katakana: ミャ ミュ ミョ
Katakana: リャ リュ リョ
Katakana: ギャ ギュ ギョ
Katakana: ジャ ジュ ジョ
Katakana: ビャ ビュ ビョ
Katakana: ピャ ピュ ピョ
Katakana: ヂャ ヂュ ヂョ
lessons.note: Rare forms, included only so you can read them. They sound exactly like the じゃ set and are practically never the right spelling.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: ファ フィ フェ フォ
lessons.note: Japanese has only ふ in the h-row u-column, so every foreign f sound is built on フ plus a small vowel.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: ティ ディ トゥ ドゥ
lessons.note: The t/d row has no ti, tu, di or du cell — ち, つ, ぢ, づ sit there instead. Loanwords rebuild the missing sounds with テ, デ, ト, ド plus a small vowel. Note the IME keys: thi, dhi, twu, dwu.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: ウィ ウェ ウォ
lessons.note: The w-row lost wi, we and wo. Modern loanwords write them with ウ plus a small vowel, not with the historical ヰ, ヱ, ヲ.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: ヴ ヴァ ヴィ ヴェ ヴォ
lessons.note: ウ with dakuten writes a foreign v. Read it, but know that the b-row spelling (バイオリン) is now standard and far more common.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: シェ ジェ チェ
lessons.note: し, じ and ち have no e-column cell. A small ェ supplies one, and these three are the most frequent extended combinations in everyday loanwords.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: ツァ ツィ ツェ ツォ
lessons.note: ツ plus a small vowel, mostly for German and Italian names and terms.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: クァ クヮ グァ
lessons.note: kwa and gwa, which Japanese lost long ago. Most words now avoid them (カルテット, グアム), so treat these as reading knowledge.

lessons.title: Katakana extended: キェ ニェ ヒェ ミェ リェ
lessons.note: The far edge of the katakana system: consonant + small ェ forms that occur only in transcription of foreign names. Included for completeness, not for production.

lessons.title: Historical kana: ゐ ゑ ヰ ヱ
lessons.note: Off the beginner path. These four were retired from ordinary use by the 1946 spelling reform; their sounds merged with い and え. Learn to recognise them for old signage, pre-war text and brand names such as ヱビス — you will never need to write them.
